title: Passwords in one minute
subtitle: Two rules, two accounts, and one of them comes back

cards.title: Two rules, then over to you
cards.say: We have one minute, so here's the short version. The machine that guesses passwords doesn't care about your exclamation mark. What slows it down is the number of combinations it has to try. What helps it is having seen your password somewhere else already.

rules.headline: Long beats clever.
rules.body: Four unrelated words. A short password stays short, however many symbols you stuff into it.

rules.headline: Never the same one twice.
rules.body: A leak on one site puts them all at risk, because attackers try the username-and-password pairs they already have everywhere else.

cards.sign_off: The full lesson adds two more rules and five password managers to choose from. This is the one-minute version.

sections.question: How are you feeling about all this?

levels.label: Still unsure
levels.reply: Nothing to worry about. Only two accounts, and nothing you type here opens anything, anywhere.

levels.label: Getting there
levels.reply: Good. Prove it on two accounts, and save them as you go.

levels.label: Confident
levels.reply: Ah, confidence. Two accounts will be a formality, then. I'll be waiting at the end to tell you which one I'd have tried first.

cards.title: Now, the proof
cards.say: Two made-up sites, one of them storing a card number. Invent a new password for each. We keep a scrambled fingerprint so you can log back in, and nothing else: not the password, not a hint, nothing we could remind you with.

rules.headline: Two sites, two new passwords.
rules.body: Both made up, both ours, and they unlock nothing. Don't use any of your real passwords, not even once.

rules.headline: We'll ask for one of them back.
rules.body: In a moment, one of the two, picked at random. We won't say which, so you'll need to have saved both.

cards.sign_off: Two accounts. Then we'll know whether the habit is real.
